To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(13)C-SIP and activity experiments revealed the presence of heterotrophic bacteria in Baltic Sea redoxclines that were previously unknown to be active in these environments.
(13)C-SIP and incubations of Baltic Sea redoxclines revealed the heterotrophic bacteria Colwellia and Arcobacter as key players in manganese and iron reduction, respectively.
acetate-utilizing bacteria were identified by stable isotope probing at an oxic anoxic interface of the Baltic Sea.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the heterotrophic bacteria that are active at pelagic redox interfaces in a stratified sea.

the identification and functional characterization of active heterotrophic bacteria in Baltic Sea pelagic anoxic waters and provides a basis for future studies of the role of these bacteria in the biogeochemical cycling of manganese and sulfur in the Baltic Sea.
a better understanding of the biogeochemical role of heterotrophic bacteria at pelagic redox interfaces.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the oxic-anoxide interface of the Baltic Sea harbors a complex microbial community, which is able to utilize a wide range of organic substrates and to reduce manganese and iron, which is of relevance for the biogeochemical cycling of these elements.
Colwellia and Arcobacter are important heterotrophic organisms in Baltic Sea redoxclines.
the oxic-anoxide interface is a habitat for a diverse community of active heterotrophic bacteria.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
heterotrophic bacteria at pelagic redoxcline layers are active, diverse, and potentially involved in metal cycling.
heterotrophs of the pelagic redoxcline are not limited to the oxic-anoxide interface but also thrive in the oxic and anoxic waters.
the oxic-anoxice interface is a habitat of a diverse bacterial community with a high potential for organic matter turnover.
The main takeaway from our work is that
heterotrophic microorganisms at pelagic redox interfaces are not only important for carbon cycling but also for the cycling of other redox-active elements, such as manganese.
the Baltic Sea is a highly productive ecosystem, with many organisms that are not yet well studied.
the heterotrophic community of the Baltic Sea pelagic oxic-anoxic transition zone is composed of bacteria that can utilize a wide variety of substrates.
